title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: All of Moscow was in the church — every friend and relation; and through the ceremony of plighting troth, in the brilliantly lit church, there was a steady flow of discreet, lowered conversation in the circle of brightly dressed women and girls and the men in white ties, frock coats, and uniforms. The talking was kept up mainly by the men, while the women were absorbed in following every detail of the ceremony, which always means so much to them.
In the small group closest to the bride were her two sisters: Dolly, and the other one, the self-possessed beauty Madame Lvova, who had only just arrived from abroad.
"Why is Marie wearing lilac — practically as bad as black — at a wedding?" said Madame Korsunskaya.
"With her coloring, it's her only salvation," Madame Trubetskaya replied. "I wonder why they had the wedding in the evening? It's a shopkeeper kind of thing...."

"It's much prettier. I was married in the evening too..." answered Madame Korsunskaya, and she sighed, remembering how charming she had looked that day, and how absurdly in love her husband had been, and how different everything was now.

"They say if a man's best man more than ten times, he'll never marry. I wanted to make it my tenth, but the spot was already taken," said Count Siniavin to the pretty Princess Tcharskaya, who had her sights on him.

Princess Tcharskaya only answered with a smile. She was looking at Kitty, thinking about how and when she would stand in Kitty's place beside Count Siniavin, and how she would then remind him of his joke today.
Shtcherbatsky told the old maid of honor, Madame Nikolaeva, that he meant to set the crown on Kitty's chignon for luck.

"She shouldn't have worn a chignon," Madame Nikolaeva answered — she had long since made up her mind that if the elderly widower she was angling for ever married her, the wedding would be of the simplest sort. "I don't care for that kind of grandeur."

Sergey Ivanovitch was talking to Darya Dmitrievna, half-joking with her that the custom of going away after the wedding was becoming common because newly married people always felt a little ashamed of themselves.
"Your brother can be proud of himself. She's a marvel of sweetness. I believe you're envious."
"Oh, I'm over that, Darya Dmitrievna," he answered, and a melancholy, serious look suddenly came over his face.
Stepan Arkadyevitch was telling his sister-in-law his joke about divorce.
"The wreath needs straightening," she answered, not hearing him.
"What a shame she's lost her looks so badly," Countess Nordston said to Madame Lvova. "Still, he's not worth her little finger, is he?"

"Oh, I like him so much — and not just because he's my future _beau-frère_," Madame Lvova answered. "And how well he's handling himself! It's so hard, too, to come off well in a position like that — not to look ridiculous. And he isn't ridiculous, and he isn't putting anything on; you can see he's moved."
"You expected this, I take it?"
"More or less. She always cared for him."
"Well, we'll see which of them steps on the rug first. I warned Kitty."
"It will make no difference," said Madame Lvova; "we're all obedient wives — it runs in the family."
"Oh, I stepped on the rug before Vassily on purpose. And you, Dolly?"

Dolly was standing next to them; she heard them, but did not answer. She was deeply moved. The tears stood in her eyes, and she could not have spoken without crying. She was rejoicing for Kitty and Levin; thinking back to her own wedding, she glanced at Stepan Arkadyevitch's radiant figure, forgot the present entirely, and remembered only her own innocent love. She thought not only of herself but of all her women friends and acquaintances. She thought of them on that one day of their triumph, when each had stood like Kitty under the wedding crown, with love and hope and dread in her heart, renouncing the past and stepping forward into the mysterious future. Among the brides who came back to her memory she thought too of her darling Anna, whose proposed divorce she had just been hearing about. And she had stood there just as innocently in orange blossoms and a bridal veil. And now? "It's terribly strange," she said to herself. It was not only the sisters, women friends, and female relations of the bride who were following every detail of the ceremony. Women who were complete strangers, mere spectators, were watching it with excitement, holding their breath, afraid of missing a single movement or expression of the bride and bridegroom, and angrily not answering — often not even hearing — the remarks of the unfeeling men, who kept making joking or off-topic observations.
"Why has she been crying? Is she being married against her will?"
"Against her will, to a fine fellow like that? A prince, isn't he?"
"Is that her sister in the white satin? Just listen to the deacon boom out, 'And fearing her husband.'"
"Are the choristers from Tchudovo?"
"No, from the Synod."
"I asked the footman. He says he's taking her straight off to his country place. Frightfully rich, they say. That's why she's marrying him."
"No, they're a well-matched pair."

"I say, Marya Vassilievna, you were claiming those fly-away crinolines weren't being worn anymore. Just look at her in the puce dress — an ambassador's wife, they say — see how her skirt bounces side to side!"
"What a pretty dear the bride is — like a lamb decked in flowers! Well, say what you like, we women feel for our sister."
Such were the comments in the crowd of gawking women who had managed to slip in at the church doors.
